text: Chapters 1 through 6 gave you the actual material an architecture review runs on — pillar tradeoffs, landing zones, network topology, disaster recovery, governance, and the ADR that records why you chose what you chose. This lesson is the last mile: turning that material into a presentation a review board can follow, question, and approve in one sitting, instead of a slide-by-slide tour of what you built.

A review deck follows five sections, in this exact order, because each one does a specific job. Problem and requirements comes first, so the room agrees on what's being solved before you show how. Options considered comes next — real alternatives, each with a one-line reason it lost — which is the single highest-leverage slide in the deck, because it answers 'did you consider X' before anyone asks it. Only then does the recommended design appear, landing as a conclusion instead of an assertion. Tradeoffs and risks get named explicitly, in the pillar language from Chapter 1. And the rollout plan closes it out: the staged path to the end state, with a rollback option if a stage fails.

Condense that structure and it fits on one page: state the problem, list two or three real options, name the recommendation, name what it costs you, and lay out how it actually gets built — shadow traffic, a percentage rollout, and a named rollback switch. That one-pager is also the direct output of the ADR work from Chapter 6; you're not writing new material for the review, you're resequencing material you already have.

Skip that order and the meeting goes sideways in predictable ways. Lead with the design before the problem is agreed, and the room re-derives requirements live, usually disagreeing with assumptions you'd already baked in. Bury the tradeoffs, or leave them out, and an experienced board finds them anyway — now you're reacting instead of having already addressed it. And a design with no rollout plan reads as an end state with no path to get there, which is exactly the gap a review exists to catch before budget and migration effort get committed.

Get the structure right and the deck does half the defending for you before a single question is asked. Next lesson picks up exactly where tradeoffs and risks leave off — the specific, predictable questions a review board asks about failure modes, cost at scale, security blast radius, and the simplest version of the design, and how to walk in already having answered them.
